{"id":"mimid-604m.5","title":"A write-ahead log is 4x fewer fsyncs and costs secure_delete's promptness","description":"A write-ahead log on the agent's database cuts the fsyncs of one first
private message from 192 to 49 and, under a deliberate I/O load, its
latency from 35.8 seconds to 11.2. It also breaks
`a_destroyed_chat_takes_its_messages_bans_and_attachments`
(crates/mimid-agent-jmap/tests/chat_delete.rs:528), which reads the raw
`mimid.sqlite` and requires that a destroyed chat's text is not in it.
That trade is Mark's, not an agent's, so the change was reverted and
measured instead (bead mimid-604m.2 holds the numbers).

## What was measured

One first private message over IRC, one provider, two daemons, counted
with `strace -f -y -T -ttt` around the test binary:

| | rollback journal (today) | write-ahead log |
|---|---|---|
| fsyncs, the two agent databases | 192 | 49 |
| journal files created and unlinked | 48 | 0 |
| directory fsyncs | 48 | 0 |
| write transactions | 48 | 48, unchanged |
| echo at the client, under load | 35.8 s | 11.2 s |
| echo at the client, idle-ish | 1.39 s | 0.65 s |

Four fsyncs per commit against one. The provider's own store already
sets `journal_mode = WAL` (mimid-server `store/mod.rs:133`) and spent 19
fsyncs on the same message.

## Why the log costs the property

`PRAGMA secure_delete` zeroes a freed page, and in a rollback journal
that zeroed page reaches `mimid.sqlite` at the commit: the text is out
of the file as soon as the delete commits, and the journal that held it
is unlinked. With a log, the zeroed page sits in `mimid.sqlite-wal`
until a checkpoint copies it back, so the old page stays in the database
file until then, and the frame that first carried the text stays in the
log file until the log is reset. SQLite checkpoints when the last
connection closes, so after a clean stop of the daemon the property
holds again; it is a running daemon, and a daemon killed, that keep the
text.

This is not only about deletes. Every overwrite is deferred, so an
edited message's old body lives in the file for a checkpoint too. A
checkpoint after each save that deleted a row would make the test pass
without restoring the whole property, which is worse than either
choice made openly.

## The choices

1. **Keep the rollback journal.** The property holds at each commit.
   Every user action pays four fsyncs a commit, and on a loaded device
   a first private message takes half a minute.
2. **Take the log, and say what it means.** Amend §7.9's promise to
   what a log gives: the text leaves the file at the next checkpoint,
   and at the latest when the daemon stops cleanly. Cheapest, and
   honest only if the promise is rewritten and the test with it.
3. **Take the log and checkpoint where the promise is made.**
   `wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE)` after the save of a destroy, with
   `journal_size_limit = 0` so the log file is truncated and not just
   reset. Keeps the promise for a destroyed chat, not for every
   overwrite, and costs a checkpoint per destroy.
4. **Leave the mode alone and attack the count.** 36 write transactions
   for one user action is the other half of the multiplier. Each is an
   MLS step and a crash cut point the outbox is built on, so this is a
   durability change, not a refactor.

## What depends on this

Bead mimid-604m: "nothing ever should hang, lock up, or go silent when
sent something to process". The first private message is the worst path
measured so far, and the journalling mode is the largest single lever on
it.
